Key takeaways. Let's recap the main points. The Stanislavski System. Constantin Stanislavski developed the first systematic approach to realistic acting in Russia in the early twentieth century. His system asks actors to find parallels between their own emotional experiences and their characters' situations, using personal memory to access authentic feeling. Actors identify their character's objective — what they want in each scene — and pursue it actively against resistance. The system transformed Western acting by making internal psychological truth the foundation of performance rather than stylized external expression or theatrical declamation. Method Acting. American teachers Lee Strasberg, Stella Adler, and Sanford Meisner each developed the Stanislavski system differently. Strasberg's Method emphasized emotional memory, asking actors to recall personal experiences to generate genuine emotion on stage or screen. Critics argued this approach was psychologically dangerous and produced self-indulgent performances. Marlon Brando, Dustin Hoffman, and Robert De Niro developed distinctive styles rooted in Method principles. The approach remains controversial but profoundly shaped American film acting's emphasis on psychological realism. Meisner Technique. Sanford Meisner disagreed with Strasberg's focus on memory, arguing that the actor's imagination should create reality rather than personal trauma. Meisner's foundational exercise has actors repeat observations about each other, discovering how genuine moment-to-moment responsiveness creates compelling performance. His famous dictum is to live truthfully in imaginary circumstances. The Meisner technique emphasizes listening and reacting authentically to partners rather than executing pre-planned choices, producing performances with genuine spontaneity and presence. Physical Theatre. Physical theatre traditions, including those from Jacques Lecoq's Paris school, develop actors through physical discipline rather than psychological excavation. Actors work with masks, which eliminate facial expression and demand the body communicate everything. Movement styles including commedia dell'arte, clown, and mime build physical vocabulary and presence. This approach complements text-based training by developing performers with strong bodies, spatial awareness, and physical expressiveness. Film actors trained in physical theatre often bring distinctive presence and economy of movement to their performances. Audition Strategies. Auditions are job interviews conducted through performance. Actors choose material that suits their type and demonstrates range within it. Self-tape auditions now dominate the industry, requiring actors to create professional-quality video with appropriate framing and sound. Casting directors see hundreds of auditions; choices that are specific, committed, and avoid obvious interpretations of material are memorable. Actors who prepare thoroughly and then release attachment to outcomes perform best. The audition is a performance, not a supplication. Memorizing Lines. Line memorization techniques range from rote repetition to associating words with physical actions and spatial locations. The most effective approach integrates line learning with understanding why each word exists in each moment — text that is understood emotionally is retained more reliably than mechanically memorized words. Off-book rehearsal begins actors discovering physical and emotional specificity impossible when holding scripts. Some actors learn lines through repeated reading rather than active drilling, trusting that comprehension creates retention through genuine engagement. Working with Directors. The actor-director relationship requires mutual trust and clear communication. Actors should ask questions that help them perform rather than seeking approval or challenging choices. Directors rarely want to explain everything — they need actors who take strong positions they can adjust. When notes are given, actors incorporate them immediately and specifically. On film sets, the director has final authority and time pressure is real; actors who prepare thoroughly, take direction efficiently, and remain flexible within their performance are invaluable collaborators. Camera Acting vs Stage Acting. Stage acting must project to the back of large auditoriums; film acting must withstand the scrutiny of extreme close-up magnified on enormous screens. Stage actors project vocally and physically; film actors find the thought, knowing the microphone and camera will capture subtlety invisible in theater. Television acting requires hitting marks precisely for camera, film acting rewards genuine spontaneous moments. Actors transitioning between mediums must recalibrate their scale constantly. The camera rewards inner life — what an actor thinks and feels registers even when their face barely moves. Keep these in mind, and you'll have a solid working grasp of Acting Techniques. Key takeaways. Let's recap the main points. What Is Accounting. Accounting is the systematic recording, summarizing, and reporting of financial transactions to enable decision-making by owners, investors, creditors, and regulators. Often called the language of business, accounting translates the economic reality of an organization into standardized numerical reports. Financial accounting produces reports for external users like shareholders and tax authorities. Management accounting produces internal reports for organizational decision-making. Every business transaction, a sale, a purchase, or a loan, has an accounting consequence that must be recorded to maintain an accurate picture of financial position. The Accounting Equation. The fundamental accounting equation is Assets equals Liabilities plus Equity. This equation must always balance because every transaction affects at least two accounts in a way that maintains this balance, which is why the system is called double-entry bookkeeping. When you buy equipment worth ten thousand dollars using cash, assets remain unchanged because cash decreases but equipment increases by the same amount. When you borrow money, both assets and liabilities increase equally. This elegant constraint ensures internal consistency in financial records and makes errors detectable through the imbalance they create. Assets Liabilities Equity. Assets are resources the business owns or controls that have future economic value: cash, inventory, equipment, buildings, accounts receivable, and intangible assets like patents. Liabilities are obligations the business owes to others: loans, accounts payable owed to suppliers, wages owed to employees, and taxes owed to authorities. Equity represents the owners' residual interest in assets after all liabilities are paid. Equity increases through profits and owner investment; it decreases through losses and owner withdrawals. Understanding these three categories is the foundation of reading any financial statement accurately. Revenue and Expenses. Revenue is income earned from the business's primary activities, selling products or providing services. Expenses are costs incurred in generating that revenue including salaries, rent, materials, utilities, and depreciation of equipment. Net income, or profit, is revenue minus expenses. Accrual accounting records revenue when it is earned and expenses when they are incurred, regardless of when cash actually changes hands. A business that delivered a service in December records that revenue in December even if payment arrives in January. This matching principle provides a truer picture of economic performance for any period. The Income Statement. The income statement, also called the profit and loss statement, summarizes revenue and expenses over a specific period: a month, quarter, or year. It begins with gross revenue, subtracts the direct costs of producing goods or services to arrive at gross profit, then subtracts operating expenses like rent and salaries to reach operating income. Interest expense and taxes are subtracted to arrive at net income. A profitable business shows positive net income; a loss-making business shows a negative result. Investors and managers analyze income statements to assess efficiency, profitability trends, and the sustainability of earnings. The Balance Sheet. The balance sheet provides a snapshot of a business's financial position at a specific moment in time, listing all assets, liabilities, and equity. Unlike the income statement, which covers a period, the balance sheet captures a single point. Current assets like cash and inventory convert to cash within a year. Long-term assets like equipment and property provide value over multiple years. Current liabilities are due within a year; long-term liabilities extend beyond that. The balance sheet reveals whether a business can pay its near-term obligations and how its resources are deployed across the organization. Cash Flow Statement. The cash flow statement tracks how cash actually moved in and out of the business during a period, divided into three sections. Operating activities show cash generated or consumed by the core business operations. Investing activities show cash spent on or received from long-term assets. Financing activities show cash from or paid to debt and equity providers. A business can report accounting profit while experiencing negative cash flow if customers are slow to pay. The cash flow statement is often considered the most reliable financial statement because cash is harder to manipulate than accrual accounting entries. Why Accounting Matters. Accounting enables every stakeholder in a business to make informed decisions based on shared, standardized information. Owners use accounting data to evaluate performance and make strategic decisions. Investors use financial statements to assess whether a business merits investment. Lenders evaluate creditworthiness from balance sheet strength and cash flow. Tax authorities ensure businesses report income accurately. Within organizations, management accounting helps managers allocate resources to the most profitable activities, control costs, and plan for future periods. Without reliable accounting, businesses cannot know whether they are profitable or whether they can meet upcoming financial obligations.
